10072-english-housewifry-exemplified-in-:
Elizabeth Moxon's English Housewifry gives directions in most parts of cookery in above four hundred and fifty receipts. It teaches soups, cakes, made-dishes, creams, pastes, jellies, pickles, and made-wines, with cuts showing the orderly placing of dishes and courses.

Bills of fare for every month in the year and an alphabetical index complete the book. Moxon calls it necessary for mistresses of families and women servants, confined to things useful, substantial, and splendid. Cooks and historians get eighteenth-century English housekeeping in full, practical detail. Her receipts cover the whole household year.
10097-the-healing-of-nations-and-the-hid:
Edward Carpenter's 1915 book, taking its epigraph from the Tree of Life whose leaves are for the healing of the nations, asks why nations go to war. Chapters examine war-madness, the roots of the Great War, and the case against Germany set beside the case for Germany.

Later chapters weigh patriotism and internationalism, the psychology of war and recruiting, conscription, commercial prosperity as the prosperity of a class, colonies and seaports, and the over-population scare. Carpenter writes as a socialist and pacifist. Readers get a wartime argument for peace, searching and unconventional.
19936-willie-the-waif:
Willie the Waif is a street-child tale in the Hesba Stretton tradition. Its waifs live in rooms they never think to clean. They had never seen their rooms any other way. Dirt had become invisible to them through habit. The pathos of that blindness is the tale's engine. A waif's story promised rescue, reform, or a pious death. Victorian readers wept over such books by the thousand.

Street Arab fiction campaigned for real children's charities. Waifs sold papers, slept in alleys, and died young in fact. Fiction turned those facts into Sunday reading. Willie's story follows the era's tender formula closely. Sentiment here had a social purpose: loosening purse strings. The book is a window into Victorian child-saving feeling.
22890-the-worlds-of-if:
Near disaster haunts The Worlds of If, a story built on a narrow escape. Its narrator reads the evening papers with relief. The liner Baikal, skirting a storm along the eastbound route, had collided mid-air with a British freighter. Only a fifth of her five hundred passengers survived the crash.

He had almost become the late Mr. Wells in a grimmer sense, he jokes, and that joke frames the tale's game with alternate outcomes. What nearly happened matters as much as what did. Stories of this type taught early science fiction readers to think in branching chances. The sea of the air, great liners, and luck fill out a brisk, thoughtful piece.
33241-letters-of-a-lunatic-a-brief-expos:
G. J. Adler's letters tell, in his own words, a strange break in his university life during 1853 and 1854. A professor of German literature in New York, Adler writes of his absence from his proper place of study and of the events that led him away from it. The letters mix personal account with learned allusion, as he tries to set down what happened and why it bore so hard on him.

Printed for the author in 1854, the book is a rare first-person record of a scholar's crisis in the mid-nineteenth century. It reads less as a formal memoir than as a plea to be heard fairly, with dates, names, and scenes set out in plain order. Readers gain a vivid glimpse of academic life, mental strain, and one man's effort to explain himself to the public.
34278-the-secrets-of-potsdam-a-startling:
The Secrets of Potsdam claims to expose the inner life of the courts of the Kaiser and the Crown Prince. The source is Count Ernst von Heltzendorff, a late personal adjutant to the German Crown Prince. William Le Queux chronicled the account. It came out in London in March 1917, in the middle of the First World War, and ran to a second impression the same month. A letter from the count, dated February 1917 from France, opens the book.

Readers should treat the volume as wartime exposure literature: it promises scandal and inside knowledge of an enemy court. Whether every claim holds up is another matter. It shows what British readers in 1917 wanted to believe about the German royal house.
35418-lewis-carroll-in-wonderland-and-at:
Belle Moses wrote the life tale of Lewis Carroll at work and at home. The book came out in New York in 1910. Moses had wrote a life of Louisa May Alcott as well. A front plate shows Carroll in a calm, grave pose. She gave the book to two friends named by first marks only.

Her front words say Carroll found a new land on a boat trip. He rowed up and down the river and told a tale as oars dipped. That land took its place in the mind's map for good. No one was quite like him, she tells his friends. The book traces the man behind Alice with warm care.
41012-the-wonderful-story-of-washington-:
The Wonderful Story of Washington and the Meaning of His Life for the Youth and Patriotism of America was written by C. Stevens and copyrighted in nineteen seventeen by Cupples and Leon of New York. Stevens also wrote the Wonderful Story of Lincoln, and the volume joins an Inspiration Series of Patriotic Americans. It opens under a long Webster passage urging American youth to hold up Washington's bright model and study his virtues.

The chapters begin with the meaning of America and Washington's early ground. They follow the boy with a will and a way into border warfare, the struggle for Fort Duquesne, and the slow separation that began between the colonies and England.
41896-dave-fearless-and-the-cave-of-myst:
Dave Fearless and the Cave of Mystery, or Adrift on the Pacific, is a boys sea tale by Rockwood. He had writ past books of the same lad, on a sunk hoard and a float isle. Prints fill this form, put out at New York in the last year of the great war.

Its rights were set in law that same year. A print at its front shows a high cliff and a call to a chief. Its parts run like a yarn log: a fine luck, foul play, a strange named man, and a pair of plot men. A doctors chance harm, a pilots plot, a queer jar, and a foe out wit fill the mid run. A bold plan, a wood isle, and a race for life lead to the sea cast.
48804-common-sense-in-the-household-a-ma:
Marion Harland wrote Common Sense in the Household, a manual of practical housewifery first entered for copyright in 1871. The revised edition here was published in New York in 1883. Harland dedicates the book to fellow housekeepers north, east, south, and west. She calls it the gleanings of many years at the stove and table.

Nearly one hundred thousand copies had worn out the first plates, she reports. New receipts are added, and old ones made clearer in light of later practice. The book teaches by doing, as its Dickens epigraph insists. Soups, meats, breads, and sweets fill a working kitchen guide. Harland's plain counsel helped shape the American cookbook shelf.
52654-the-autobiography-of-goethe-truth-:
The Autobiography of Goethe, in English as Truth and Poetry from My Own Life, is Goethe's account of his own early life. John Oxenford translated it from the German. The revised edition here, from George Bell and Sons in 1897, holds Books One through Twenty in one volume.

An opening note tells the care behind the text. The first ten books had come out in America, but the publisher found that version not faithful enough to the German. Oxenford made a fresh translation, though he kept good renderings from the older one where he found them. The note also weighs the title: Truth and Poetry is the nearest English for Wahrheit und Dichtung. Goethe's own preface follows. For the reader, the book gives the poet's growth in his own words, shaped late in life out of fact and art together.
54151-shakespeare-the-boy-with-sketches-:
William James Rolfe wrote Shakespeare the Boy, with a copyright of 1896 and a London printing in 1897. Rolfe was a noted editor of Shakespeare for schools. His aim here is to show the lad behind the plays by showing the world that raised him in Warwickshire.

Forty-one pictures show the town, the castle at Warwick, and Kenilworth. Rolfe sketches home life, school life, games, and sports of the time. Manners, customs, and folk-lore fill out the picture, with tales such as Guy of Warwick. Young readers get the England of the boy Shakespeare, the soil from which the plays grew, told in plain and friendly terms.
57667-the-changing-world-and-lectures-to:
Annie Besant lectures in The Changing World and Lectures to Theosophical Students: fifteen lectures delivered in London during May, June, and July 1909. The Theosophical Book Concern of Chicago and the Theosophical Publishing Society of London issued them in 1910. Besant was president of the Theosophical Society.

Part one, lectures to the public, opens with the deadlock in religion, science, and art. It turns to the new doors opening, brotherhood applied to social conditions, the coming race, and the coming Christ. Part two speaks to students: the sixth sub-race, the sacramental life, and the nature of the Christ.
62745-dissertation-on-the-gipseys-repres:
H M G Grellmann's German study of the Gypsy people reached English readers in a new form in 1807. William Ballintine printed it at London. This printing trims the heavy notes of the first translation by M Raper.

The contents map a whole way of life. Early chapters treat names, food, and drink. Then come dress, family economy, and trades. Marriages and schooling follow. Sickness, death, and burial get their own chapters. Grellmann also asks where this people came from. His closing enquiry traces their origin and first steps into Europe. The work shaped how Europe saw the Romani for a century. Modern readers use it with care, as a record of its age as much as of its subject.
64345-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art began its fifth series with number one on Saturday, January 5, 1884. William and Robert Chambers had founded the journal in 1832. This issue, priced at three halfpence, opens with a story called By Mead and Stream, by Charles Gibbon, author of Robin Gray.

Gibbon's first chapter, headed Much Virtue in If, muses on lives looking back from a hilltop. Old friends meet and sigh over the word if: the road not taken, the advice not given in time. The scene sets a reflective tone for a weekly that mixed fiction with science and art for family reading. The Chambers firm built its name on cheap, improving print for the new reading public.
64475-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, for Saturday 12 January 1884, is number two of the first volume of its fifth series. The paper was set up by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. It was run by R. Chambers the second, and sold for a penny halfpenny. The lead piece asks a plain question: What is a peer?

Many folk seem to think, the piece says, that each man called Lord So-and-so is a peer. That notion is wholly wrong, it holds. The peerage of this realm, unlike that of other lands, is a matter of real weight, in a social and in a state sense. So an answer to the question may not prove dull, the piece goes on. The word peer itself, in its root sense, hints at no high place at all, it notes with surprise.
64571-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number three of its fifth series, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, January 19, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. The price was three halfpence. The lead article is an essay on the training of girls, wives, and mothers among the middle classes.

The writer grants that higher culture for women draws much sympathy in theory. In practice, the essay warns, schools give drawing room polish at the cost of home skill. Young housewives gain too much of the stage and too little of the kitchen. The author argues that training should fit women for the battle of life. For middle class women, those years of battle come after marriage, not before. Education, on this view, must not end at the altar.
64962-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal gave London readers a cheap weekly of tale and fact. Issue five of the fifth series is dated February 2, 1884. It sold for one and a half pence. William and Robert Chambers set the paper up in 1832. A younger Chambers ran it at this date.

Hampstead Heath leads with tales of boy days on its wild edge. Ass rides and wild rides through fern scared nurses then, it says. The old town on the hill still keeps its own ways, it holds. A fifth of November march winds its steep streets each year. More tale and science bits fill the rest.
64975-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, fifth series, number six, is dated Saturday, February 9, 1884, and sold for three halfpence. The journal was established by William and Robert Chambers in 1832 and was now conducted by a second Chambers of the name. Circulating-Library Critics is the lead paper of the number.

It appears to be a mania with some people, the paper begins, to criticise everything that comes in their way. The last new bonnet, a pug dog, or the last new novel all take their turn. Its chosen specimen is the subscriber to a circulating library, who cuts up every author he reads in pencilled margins. Some notes are uncalled for, some personal, and some so ridiculous that a later reader underlines them in sarcasm. The journal's tone is the thing: dry, amused, and shrewd.
64993-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 7 of volume I, fifth series, is a weekly number dated Saturday, February 16, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. R Chambers (Secundus) conducted this series. The price was three-halfpence. The number leads with an article on life assurance: How Life-Offices Pay Their Death-Claims.

The article answers an old objection to life assurance, the delay in paying claims. Offices now vie, it says, in prompt settlement. Policies already provide some four hundred and thirty-five millions sterling for future widows and orphans. That figure excludes industrial business. The writer marvels at the alleviation of misery the sum represents. Cottages and stately halls alike draw on the beneficent treasury. Popular misunderstandings still abound, the article notes. One man proposed to draw half his assurance at once. Another asked to let his premiums run as a debt against the policy.
64994-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 4 of its fifth series, is dated Saturday, January 26, 1884. William and Robert Chambers founded the weekly in 1832. R Chambers, the second of that name, now conducts it. The number leads with an editorial, Another Word to Literary Beginners. The editors address the great class knocking weekly at literature's doors.

They back the warning with their own submission figures. From August 1882 to August 1883 they received 3,225 manuscripts. Of these, 2,065 were prose and 1,160 verse. They accepted 300 prose pieces, about fourteen per cent. Only 30 poems passed, under three per cent. Ten of every hundred manuscripts were kept, and ninety returned. The offerings came from across the English-speaking world. They ranged from a few stanzas to a three-volume novel. The editorial urges encouragement within limits. Most aspirants, it warns, harvest only disappointment and heart-sickness.
65015-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, February 23, 1884, is number eight of the first volume of its fifth series. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832, and it sold for three halfpence. Popular literature, science, and art fill its stated scope.

The number leads with Our Health, a lecture series by Andrew Wilson, a health lecturer. Health, Wilson says, is the smooth working of all the body's organs in concert. A broken bone breaks that harmony just as a fever does, and an aching tooth counts as much as a brain disorder. Life hangs on surroundings, he notes, and those can turn from support to source of disease. Pure air and clean water, both needs of life, can carry sickness when fouled. The lecture sets out to teach readers their own machinery.
65133-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 10 of the fifth series, is a weekly magazine issue. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in the year 1832. Chambers the second conducted this series from Edinburgh in Scotland. This number is dated Saturday, March 8, 1884, at three halfpence. Nettle Cloth, its lead article, opens on a botanist's remark.

A famous botanist was asked about gathering all plants used in medicine. Such a hoard would take a large building to hold, he replied. Fibre yielding plants would still form a long list for study. Very few serve for clothing among civilised and savage races alike. Cotton and flax hold prime importance, the article argues, with hemp rising.
65209-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number eleven of its fifth series, volume one, for Saturday, March 15, 1884, cost three halfpence. The journal, established by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, was now conducted by Chambers the second. The opening story is called Happy Ever After.

By firelight, the children had heard a traveller's tale of the desert mirage: the distant vision of tufted palms and green herbage, the promise of water, shade, and rest. They had heard how the delusion flies, baffling pursuit, always seeming at an attainable distance, always infinitely far. The story turns that mirage into a parable of hoping. Around it the journal packs its usual Saturday mix of tale, essay, and fact. Two generations of families read Chambers's as a matter of course.
65239-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number twelve of its fifth series, is a weekly issue dated Saturday, March 22, 1884. The journal had been founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. The price was three halfpence. The lead article reports on the gold fields of the Transvaal, written by a man on the spot.

The writer says the fields have drawn fresh notice at home and in South Africa. Gold lies scattered over a wide country, reaching toward the Zambesi river. The busiest belt runs from the Kaap River north past Pilgrim's Rest. Named farms there have yielded the largest amounts so far. Most gold found is loose in the soil and won by washing with water. Two companies were starting to crush quartz rock with machines when he wrote.
65279-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal dated this weekly number Saturday, March 29, 1884, in its fifth series, first volume. The paper had been founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. Its lead article turns to the International Forestry Exhibition planned for Edinburgh in 1884.

The writer begins with the age of great exhibitions, which newspapers call a wholesome mania. He asks what calls such shows into being and what good their backers expect from them. Towns, host countries and all the nations taking part stand to gain, he argues, if the show is well aimed and honestly run.
65338-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal offers this earlier number of its fifth series, number 14 of the first volume, for Saturday, April 5, 1884. The price is again three halfpence. A long essay on gold leads the issue, opening with the fable of Midas and his ruinous touch.

Gold, the essay argues, is greater than money, since on gold the whole frame of the world's wealth rests. It is scarce, and scarcity is the first root of value. Yet gold would not fall to iron's price if it grew common, for no other metal matches its uses. It never rusts, melts clean, and beats out to leaves a grain of which can cover fifty-six square inches. Egyptian digs and Schliemann's finds prove its endless life. The essay marches from myth to mint with a Scotch magazine's confidence. Family reading, solidly gilded.
65389-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art was a penny and a half weekly founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. This number, dated Saturday, April 12, 1884, belongs to the journal's fifth series. Its lead article treats nature around London.

Most people, the article begins, think country sights and sounds lie far from the great city. Richard Jefferies, in his book Nature near London, showed that to be a mistake. Twelve miles out lie villages in leafy copses, lanes full of bird and insect life, and streams where a great trout lay for four years in a pool under a beech tree. The journal mixed such essays with tales, science notes, and poems for family reading.
65543-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 16 of the fifth series, volume 1, was dated Saturday, April 19, 1884. The weekly, founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, was now conducted by a second Robert Chambers. The lead essay, Sudden Fortunes, opens with tales of wealth gained in a flash.

The essay notes how gold and diamond fields and big lottery prizes grip readers. When French state lotteries ended in 1837, Alphonse Karr protested that five sous bought the poorest man a chance to be a millionaire, and killing the chance killed a ray of hope. Set gains from trade or kin apart, the essay says: true sudden fortune drops, unlooked for, into a man's hands like a bird or a pearl.
65567-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, April 26, 1884, is number 17 of the fifth series, priced at a penny halfpenny. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. The lead article takes up post-office life assurance and annuities. The scheme had run since 1865 to help the poorer classes save.

Its results, the journal admits, are trifling. In nearly twenty years only six thousand five hundred and twenty-four life policies were issued. Annuity contracts reached twelve thousand four hundred and thirty-five. Live policies had sunk to four thousand six hundred and fifteen. A committee under the Postmaster-General Fawcett reported in 1882, and an act passed the same session. The new system was to start on the first of May.
65594-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art was a famed cheap weekly founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. This number, eighteen of the fifth series, came out on Saturday, May 3, 1884, priced at three halfpence, under editor R Chambers the second.

The lead article tours the Norfolk Broads and Rivers, praising a wild country of marsh, mere, and reed that many readers had never seen. It paints reedy capes, sedgy islets, and shallow bays bright with yellow iris, ragged-robin, forget-me-not, and water-lilies. A lone yacht's white sail or a wherry's red-brown canvas crosses the still scene, and the only sounds are oars and startled waterfowl. The piece draws on G Christopher Davies's book on the Broads. Such numbers brought travel, science, and story within reach of working readers each week, for the price of a loaf.
65598-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal was a cheap weekly of tales, science, and art, run by the Chambers family of Edinburgh since 1832. This number came out on Saturday, May 10, 1884, for three halfpence. Its lead piece takes up a sharp word of the day: the corner.

The writer explains how men try to corner a market, buying up a good to force its price. Most, he warns, draw back empty-handed, with loss and shame. Tales, poems, and notes on new finds fill the rest of the number. The issue shows how the journal fed plain readers both facts and fun each week.
65647-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, number 20 of its fifth series, came out on Saturday, May 17, 1884, at a penny-halfpenny. The weekly had been founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832 and was now conducted by Chambers the second. Its lead paper, Some Curiosities of the Peerage, is the first of two parts.

That earlier paper dealt with the outside of the institution: the peerage, the House of Lords, and real against courtesy titles. This paper turns inward, to the oddities known only to the few: family vicissitudes, personal anecdotes, and the strange workings of the system. The writer argues that no one can fully grasp the history of the country, general or constitutional, without knowing the peerage and how it works. Instruction, he promises, will come wrapped in amusement.
65679-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art was a weekly founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. This issue, number 21 of the fifth series, is dated Saturday, May 24, 1884, and sold for three halfpence. A trip from Jaffa to Jerusalem leads the number.

The writer tells of the Syrian shore, the scent of orange flowers borne over the sea, and the old town of Jaffa in sight at dawn. More tales, facts, and verse fill the rest, as the journal gave each week. Readers get a bright mix of travel, learning, and light reading made for the home.
65723-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 22 of the fifth series, is a weekly magazine issue. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in the year 1832. Chambers the second conducted this series from Edinburgh in Scotland. This number is dated Saturday, May 31, 1884, at three halfpence. Its lead article, Our Detective Police, opens the number's argument.

Many murders near London have gone unsolved in the last few months. Few murderers have been brought to justice in that span, it says. Thefts and burglaries beyond count go unpunished, since culprits vanish unseen. London's boast as the safest city in the world rings hollow here. A new departure in detective police is required, the writer urges.
65785-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
A weekly journal of popular reading, founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832, reached number twenty three of its fifth series on June 7, 1884. The price was three halfpence. The lead piece is a character sketch of the newsmonger. He is nothing, the writer says, if not all knowing.

When a bankruptcy bursts on the world, the newsmonger is never surprised. He knew it weeks before, down to the sum and the chief creditor. When a wife runs off, he had warned both parties. When an engagement breaks, he advised the break himself. He deals in bad news by choice, for it has the spice that good news lacks. The sketch is dry, fond, and cutting, a fair sample of the journal's fare for the fireside.
65795-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art, Fifth Series, Number 24 for June 14, 1884, was sold at three halfpence. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in 1832. R Chambers the second ran this issue. The lead piece treats St Marguerite and St Honorat, isles in the Mediterranean.

The piece notes a sad link to the Duke of Albany. His last public act was to sign a plea against the sale of St Marguerite. The isles lie in the Golfe de Frejus off Cannes. Tales of the man with the iron mask hang over St Marguerite. Old tales say a young knight from Gaul first settled the isles in early Christian days. His sister Marguerite followed him there.
65821-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal, number 25 of its fifth series, is dated Saturday, June 21, 1884. The lead piece is Nature on the Roof, by Richard Jefferies, author of The Gamekeeper at Home. Jefferies watches the housetop as closely as any wood. Starlings whistle from his ledge long before spring spray greens the hawthorn.

His pair of starlings claim a ledge between eave and window as their own. They nest between slates and wall and may rear a winter brood. Jefferies notes that the birds destroy thousands of insects and earn the farmer's thanks. The essay shows his gift: patient watching turns a London roof into a small wild world. The journal mixed such nature writing with tales and facts.
65828-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science and Art was a long-running weekly for family reading. William and Robert Chambers founded it in 1832. This number, twenty-six of the fifth series, is dated Saturday, June 28, 1884. It sold for a penny and a half in Edinburgh and London.

The lead article is Our Health, part three, by Doctor Andrew Wilson. Its subject is food dangers and how to avoid them. Alum and copper salts in bread, watered milk, and faced tea all come under attack. Green peas tinted with copper poison get hard words. Wilson argues that law against food adulteration is both needed and overdue. The journal mixed such counsel with tales and verse for the home.
65862-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art is a weekly magazine founded by William and Robert Chambers in 1832. The hosted issue opens the fifth series, dated Saturday, July 5, 1884, and priced at a penny halfpenny. It was conducted by Robert Chambers the second. The lead article is the first of a series on home nursing, written by a lady.

That article argues that illness visits every household, so care of the sick matters to all. It notes how trained nursing has lately improved, pushing out the old careless nurse of story. Yet most people still know little of bedside care, and the series aims to teach them. It stresses plain guidance so a reader can act in an emergency with some skill. The journal mixed such practical pieces with literature, science, and art for a broad public.
65881-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal, number twenty eight of the fifth series, is a weekly from July twelfth eighteen eighty four. William and Robert Chambers founded the journal in eighteen thirty two. Chambers the second conducted this series of the popular weekly. The price was three halfpence for the number that week in Britain.

The lead piece, On Moor and Loch, opens at a small Scottish station. A June morning follows a fortnight drought and two days of kind rain. Grey mist, or haar, rolls in from the German Ocean on east wind. No angler loves mist, the writer notes, for trout gain by its cover. Pentland hills loom as a darker bank in a grey waste of cloud.
65883-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal for Saturday, July 19, 1884, is the twenty-ninth number of the journal's fifth series. William and Robert Chambers founded the weekly in 1832, and it sold for three halfpence. Its lead essay is Some Cheering Aspects of Mortality. The essay takes up a grim subject with dry wit.

The writer says we always mourn what the world loses when great men die. We seldom credit what the world gains by their going. Leading men who live too long can block the way of the next generation. Even our own shoes may be better filled after us. The essay also notes that the great are often scorned in life. Distance alone lends them their glow, and honor comes only after death.
65951-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers's Journal of Popular Literature, Science, and Art is a week sheet set up by William and Robert Chambers in eighteen thirty two. The host print is count thirty of the fifth line of the sheet. It bears the date of a high day of eighteen eighty four. Its price is set at the head of the page. A man of the same name runs the sheet.

The lead piece of the week treats a Scots sea watch post. The sea, it says, has been watched for ages in more ways than men can count. Bards have sung of it, fish men have fished it, sea men have sailed it for years past count. Yet it is still a tract of doubt and awe. The lore of the sea is yet in its young years.
66007-chambers-s-journal-of-popular-lite:
Chambers Journal for a day in the summer of eighteen eighty four is one issue of a cheap weekly of tales, science, and art. This is its fifth run, set up by its two first hands in the age of Victoria as a girl. A grand son of one of them now runs the sheet.

Its lead piece is a plain talk on water. Water bears a most big part in the frame of man and the keep of health, it says. It joins with the stuff of the body and forms a need part of its build. britannica-1911-coif:
A coif is a close cap for the head, from a French word for a cap. In the middle ages men and women wore it out of doors. It tied under the chin like a night-cap. Later men kept it as a night-cap or skull-cap at home. One form of the cap gained a set place in English law.

Serjeants-at-law wore a coif of white lawn or silk as a mark of their rank. Fashion added a small black skull-cap on top of the white. britannica-1911-massif: Massif is a French term adopted in geology and in physical geography, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains in brief. Born probably at Hipswell in Yorkshire in 1324, he was educated at Balliol College and resigned its mastership in 1361 for the living of Fillingham, later exchanged for Ludgershall. From his Oxford eminence Wyclif launched the attacks on papal wealth, friars, and transubstantiation that made him famous and condemned. english-housewifry-exemplified-in-above-:
Elizabeth Moxon offers above four hundred and fifty receipts in English Housewifry, the fruit, she says, of thirty years of practice and experience. Directions cover soups, cakes, made dishes, creams, pastes, jellies, pickles, and made wines. Cuts show the orderly placing of dishes and courses, and bills of fare run for every month of the year.

Receipt 270 makes calf's foot flummery: boil two dressed feet in two quarts of water till half is consumed, then set, chill, and turn out pricked with blanched almonds. An appendix adds sixty more receipts from skilled gentlewomen nearby. Moxon writes for mistresses of families and women servants, on measures of frugality. The book stands among the plainest, most used cookbooks of its century.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ClayCassius_Cla:
Cassius Marcellus Clay of Kentucky was the nineteenth century's most combative abolitionist, a slaveholder's son who turned against slavery and fought duels over emancipation. This essay, by an unidentified author, celebrates him under the name Muhammad Ali was born with.

The essay praises Clay as 'the greatest' across fighting, editorials, and even husbands, in the loose and hearty style of a magazine tribute. Clay edited an abolitionist paper, survived attempts on his life, and lived to be a legend called the Lion of White Hall. The piece survives as popular biography, more affectionate than exact, preserved in the research files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-NavyFOIALiftonR:
The Chief of Naval Operations sent this memorandum on February 25, 1981. It refers Harold Weisberg's freedom-of-information request onward to the Navy's Bureau of Medicine and Surgery. Weisberg sought Navy medical records tied to the Kennedy autopsy, and his request had to travel to the office that held them.

Referral memos are the plumbing of the Freedom of Information Act. A request arrives at the wrong desk; the agency routes it and notes the routing. This one preserves the path of a single request in February 1981, one step in a legal campaign Weisberg had already pursued for years. The memo shows an agency processing a critic's demand through channels, three decades of paperwork still to come.
nasa-tm-19660014325-go-no-go-for-apollo-:
F O Vonbun at Goddard derived a simple rule in November 1965 for a key Apollo question: should a mission go, or not go, based on how long its orbit will last? Orbital lifetime is set by air drag, which slowly pulls a low satellite down. A short predicted life could rule out a planned mission. Vonbun gives the go, no-go test in a clean analytic form.

He says a formula teaches more than a giant computer program does. A chart in the paper compares his quick slide-rule answers with computer results. Planners gained a check they could run by hand. In a program as complex as Apollo, simple cross-checks had real value against silent machine errors.
nasa-tm-19670013545-a-method-to-correct-:
Barbara Sparkman, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, wrote this method paper in February 1967. It fixes a calibration problem in a Nimbus medium resolution infrared radiometer flown on NASA's Convair 990 research aircraft. The instrument's three infrared channels read lower and lower as the aircraft climbed, so high-altitude measurements came out too low.

Sparkman's correction leans on the radiometer's built-in check-of-calibration cavity, whose temperature is tracked by an embedded thermistor. Assuming the whole calibration shifted by the amount that check indicates, degraded readings can be repaired. The paper derives the correction equations and describes a way to test them. Data checks gave good agreement with temperatures worked out from theory, once radiation passing through the atmosphere was accounted for. A closing section explains the physical cause of the shift.
nasa-tm-19700015446-cosmic-ray-diffusion:
Frank C. Jones of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint on how cosmic rays spread through space. Cosmic rays are fast particles that slowly diffuse, wandering as they cross a region of space. Jones checks a common shortcut in that work, the leakage lifetime approximation, and asks when it can be trusted.

His tool is an expansion of the solution in eigenfunctions, the natural patterns of the governing equation. Keeping only the lowest pattern gives the shortcut, and Jones shows where that move holds up. With energy losses such as synchrotron or inverse Compton losses, he finds, it cannot be justified. He also solves the general case where several energy effects act together.
the-healing-of-nations-and-the-hidden-so: Edward Carpenter wrote The Healing of Nations and the Hidden Sources of Their Strife. The book is dated 1915. A line from Revelation stands on the title page. It speaks of the tree of life and the healing of nations. The contents list seventeen chapters. Titles include War-Madness and The Roots of the Great War. Later titles include The Case Against Germany and The Case for Germany. An appendix is called A New and Better Peace. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
